subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
passage: In the fifth-floor dev room of a logistics firm, Anjali, a junior developer, was rushing to clear a ticket before the evening stand-up. The AI tool wrote the search function in seconds, the tests turned green, and Anjali merged it without reading past the first lines. It felt like a small win. Three days later Sunaina, doing a routine pass over merged code, stopped at the query. It built its command by pasting user text straight into it, which left the search box open to tricks. Sunaina raised it with the team lead at once, the change was pulled, and the cleanup took two people a full day. Anjali sat very still at the stand-up. 'I just trusted that green meant fine,' she said quietly.

qa.q: How long after the merge did Sunaina notice the query?
qa.a: Sunaina noticed it three days later.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling at the stand-up?
qa.a: Anjali felt embarrassed and regretful, sitting very still and admitting a trust in green tests.

qa.q: What could Anjali do differently with AI-written code next time?
qa.a: Anjali could read every line, test odd inputs, and ask a colleague to review before merging, since passing basic tests does not prove the code is safe.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt on finding the query?
qa.a: Sunaina was probably concerned about the risk to users, which is why they raised it with the lead at once.

grounding: Shows a junior developer merging AI-written code unread, so an insecure query passes basic tests and reaches production before a reviewer notices.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
passage:
Dear Nitin,
You asked me to write down what happened last week, in my own words, so here it is.
On Tuesday I asked the AI assistant to write the search function for the orders page. It gave me thirty lines that looked clean. I ran the tests, they passed, and I merged it without reading it properly. It was late, and it looked like the code seniors write.
On Friday, Meenal from the security team found that the query took the user's search text straight into the database command. Someone could have typed something that showed other customers' orders. It had been live for three days. Meenal's team patched it within the hour and checked the logs; nobody had used the hole.
But it was my name on the merge. From now on I read every line and ask for a review, even at 7 p.m.
Thomas

qa.q: How long had the code been live?
How does Thomas feel about the name on the merge?
qa.a: Thomas feels ashamed and shaken, knowing the careless merge could have exposed customers' orders.

qa.q: What else could the team change so a slip like this is caught earlier?
qa.a: They could require a second reviewer for any code that builds database queries, and add security tests beyond the basic ones.

qa.q: How might Meenal see the discovery?
qa.a: Meenal may be relieved it was caught in three days and hopeful that an honest account like this helps the team learn.

grounding: It shows a junior developer merging AI-written code without reading it, so an insecure query passes basic tests and reaches production before a reviewer notices.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
passage:
Nitin, you asked why I'm suddenly so careful with the AI assistant. Okay. I'm Sunaina, junior-most on the team, and last month I let it write the login check for our admin page. It produced a neat query, the three tests passed, and I was proud of how fast I'd been. I merged it before lunch.
Two weeks later our senior reviewer, doing a routine audit, stopped at my code. The query glued the password field right into the database command. With the right characters typed in, anyone could have got into the admin page. She blocked it in ten minutes and checked the logs; nobody had used it. Then she sat with me and made me explain every line. I couldn't explain half of them. That was the worst part. Now I don't merge anything I can't explain.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel on being unable to explain half the lines?
qa.a: Sunaina felt embarrassed and shaken, realising that pride in speed had hidden a lack of understanding.

qa.q: What else could Sunaina do before merging AI-written code?
qa.a: Sunaina could ask for a review of any code touching logins or data and write a test that tries unusual input.

qa.q: How might the senior reviewer see Sunaina's mistake?
qa.a: The reviewer treats it as a serious risk but also a teaching moment, sitting down to go through every line together.

grounding: It shows a junior merging AI-written code without reading it, so an insecure query passes basic tests and goes live until a reviewer notices.
